commercial_property_rate_trend_pct.note: No single long-run trend value is defensible; the market is cyclical. Observations (NATIONAL, not Texas-specific): CIAB commercial property +20.4% (Q1 2023, the first >20% since 2001), +11.8% (Q4 2023), -6.3% (Q2 2026, the second straight quarter as the steepest-falling line). Marsh US property -13% in Q2 2026 (eighth straight quarterly decline; cat-exposed programs >$1M -20%). low/high = observed range. Recommend the model use a user-set premium escalator rather than extrapolating either the hard or the soft market. No Texas-specific commercial rate index found. All non-GitHub web sources were read only as search-engine result excerpts: direct page fetches were blocked by the research environment's egress proxy. Verify before external use.

roof_age_underwriting.text: Texas carriers increasingly settle roof losses at ACV (depreciated) rather than RCV once roofs pass an age threshold, commonly cited as 10, 15 or 20 years, with 15 most often cited in 2026 sources. Roof payment schedules pay a set percentage of roof cost by age. Commercial forms add cosmetic-damage exclusions for hail (endorsement CP 10 36 cited), which matter most for metal roofs (dents without functional failure pay $0). Exterior or aerial inspections feed non-renewal or ACV conversion. Most sources found are homeowner-focused; commercial-specific evidence is thinner (Higginbotham and Core Commercial Roofing pages were seen by title/excerpt only). Sales implication: documented maintenance and condition records (PaxSeal reports) can support insurability and RCV terms, but no source quantified a premium credit for maintained roofs. All non-GitHub web sources were read only as search-engine result excerpts: direct page fetches were blocked by the research environment's egress proxy. Verify before external use.

wind_hail_deductible_norms.text: Commercial wind/hail deductibles in Texas often range from 1% to 5% of total insured value (Lundquist Law Firm). Named-storm deductibles 2-10% of insured value (search excerpt, unattributed; less relevant inland). For Texas residential in 2026, 2% has become the dominant wind/hail deductible, with some carriers at 3%. Example: at 2% on a $10M building, the owner retains the first $200K of a hail loss, which is often more than a roof replacement, so many hail events are effectively uninsured for the roof. code_triggers.text: Model-code text (2021 IBC Sec. 1512 / 2021 IEBC Sec. 705, opened): (1) A roof RECOVER is NOT permitted where the existing roof is water-soaked or deteriorated so it is not an adequate base, where the existing covering is slate/clay/cement/asbestos-cement tile, or where the roof already has TWO OR MORE applications of any roof covering. So a neglected, wet roof forces full tear-off, and a second recover is prohibited. (2) New protective coatings over existing coatings, metal panel, BUR, SPF, mod bit, and thermoset/thermoplastic single-ply are permitted without tear-off, which is the code basis for coating/restoration. (3) Reroof/recover of low-slope roofs is exempt from the 1/4:12 minimum slope and from adding secondary drains, provided positive drainage exists; existing secondary drains may not be removed. (4) Existing rusted/damaged flashings, edge metal and drain collars and damaged ballast may not be reinstalled. NOT VERIFIED: which I-code edition and local amendments the City of San Antonio has adopted (believed to be a 2021 I-code cycle, unconfirmed), and the IECC re-roof insulation requirement (IECC C503 roof replacement: insulation upgrade where insulation is entirely above deck), whose text and R-values were not opened. Texas has no statewide commercial building code for most private buildings, so city adoption governs.

A single building is not expected to be destroyed every 4-5 yrs.
